newsitem.title: USA: Africa-bound U.S. troops will not disarm factions.
newsitem.headline: Africa-bound U.S. troops will not disarm factions.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry on Thursday said Africa-bound U.S. troops would be armed to protect themselves but not to conduct combat operations or disarm rival factions while helping to deliver aid in Zaire.

Perry told reporters the projected ground force of as many as 1,000 U.S. troops, which will be part of a Canadian-led multinational expedition, would have "robust" rules of engagement to protect themselves in eastern Zaire, where aid supplies to Rwandan refugees have been cut by fighting.

"We will have arms and have what we call robust rules of engagement to allow our forces to protect themselves" in the volatile region along the Rwanda-Zaire border, Perry said. More than one million refugees are in dire need of food, water and shelter in the area, relief workers have said.

Perry said the United States needed the "acquiesence" of rival factions in war-ravaged eastern Zaire to accomplish the international mission of delivering humanitarian aid. "We need the support and cooperation of the parties to do this," he said. "We are not planning a mission to go in and disarm factions or to separate the military from refugees."

Perry spoke at a picture-taking session with visiting Defence Minister Severin Adjori of the West African state of Benin. They were expected to discuss African participation in a possible follow-on force after the projected four-month international humanitarian effort winds up.

The White House said on Wednesday that President Bill Clinton had decided in principle to send U.S. troops and helicopters, provided the mission was of limited duration and involved other countries' forces as well.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly ethnic Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then. A new war broke out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zairians backed by Zaire's rag-tag army.

Asked whether he feared that U.S. forces might be sucked into a combat mission, Perry replied: "Our forces that go in will go in armed, and with rules of engagement that will provide for their own protection."

Despite a broad consensus that the Zaire crisis could lead to thousands of deaths without urgent action, Clinton, who was elected last week to a second term, and other U.S. officials have approached the matter with reluctance and caution.

The United States has painful memories of its involvement in a U.N. relief mission to Somalia in 1993, when 18 U.S. soldiers were killed in a firefight while pursuing a Somali warlord, prompting partisan political recriminations.

Separately, Perry said he expected Clinton to make up his mind "in the near future" on possible U.S. participation in any follow-on peacekeeping force for Bosnia to replace the U.S.-led force scheduled to wind up its mission next month.
